claims.text: A multiscale model coupling DFT electronic-structure and electron–phonon calculations with anharmonic phonon-scattering simulations can separately predict electronic and lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the electronic and lattice thermal-conductivity contributions of HfNbTaTiZr are roughly comparable.
From 300 to 1200 K, the predicted total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr will be 10–17 W/(K m).
The new model will reduce prediction errors by approximately 20–25% relative to analytical Debye or perfect-crystal methods.
The relevant material state is bulk, defect-controlled HfNbTaTiZr in a disordered solid-solution state with oxygen near 1 wt.%.
DFT can be used to evaluate the electronic heat-transport contribution, including electron–phonon coupling effects.
Anharmonic phonon calculations or molecular-dynamics-based methods can directly simulate lattice thermal transport in this alloy.
The model is applicable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K for samples having controlled oxygen content near 1 wt.%.
Configurational disorder and short-range compositional fluctuations in HfNbTaTiZr govern electron scattering.
Configurational disorder and short-range compositional fluctuations in HfNbTaTiZr govern phonon–phonon interactions.
First-principles treatment of complex local atomic environments captures strong anharmonicity and electronic-scattering effects missed by idealized defect-free Debye approaches.
Accounting for anharmonicity and electronic scattering permits separate determination of lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
The sum of the separately predicted lattice and electronic conductivities will match measured total conductivity to within 20%.
At elevated temperatures, electronic thermal transport will moderately dominate lattice thermal transport.
Earlier perfect-crystal and Debye-based conductivity estimates often have errors exceeding 40%.
The errors of earlier methods arise from their inability to capture complex scattering mechanisms in high-entropy alloys.
The predictions may not apply to nanostructured HfNbTaTiZr or to samples with substantial additional defects or compositional variation.
Frequency-domain thermoreflectance can provide the phonon contribution while Seebeck and Hall analyses can provide the electronic contribution for decisive component-resolved comparison.
A deviation greater than 20% between prediction and independently measured component conductivities, or failure to observe the predicted channel balance, would falsify the hypothesis.
